draft.title: Float time
card: Float is how long an activity can be delayed without delaying the whole project. Float = latest start time − earliest start time.
Both start times come from scans of the network, which are taught in earlier points. Here they are given, so you only subtract.
Worked example: an activity has an earliest start of 6 days and a latest start of 10 days. Float = 10 − 6 = 4 days.
A float of 4 days means the activity can start up to 4 days late and the project still finishes on time. A float of 0 means there is no room to delay it.
draft.remember: Float is latest start minus earliest start: the spare time an activity has.

a.q: An activity has an earliest start time of 8 days and a latest start time of 13 days. What is its float?
opts: 5 days
21 days
8 days
13 days
a.why: Float = latest start − earliest start = 13 − 8 = 5 days. Adding the two times gives 21, which is a sign error in the method, because float is a difference.
a.clue: Subtract the earlier start from the later one.

b.q: Priya manages a build in Newcastle. Fitting windows has an earliest start of 14 days and a latest start of 14 days. Painting has an earliest start of 9 days and a latest start of 12 days. Which statement is correct?
opts: Windows can't be delayed, and painting has 3 days float
Windows have 14 days float, and painting has 3 days
Windows can't be delayed, and painting has 12 days float
Windows have 14 days float, and painting has 21 days
b.why: Windows: 14 − 14 = 0, so any delay holds up the project. Painting: 12 − 9 = 3 days of float. Using a latest start time on its own as the float is the tempting mistake, because float is a difference.
b.clue: Work out latest start minus earliest start for each activity.

b.best: Windows can't be delayed, and painting has 3 days float

proposal.title: Float time
card: Float is how long an activity can be delayed without delaying the whole project. Float = latest start time − earliest start time.
Always subtract the earliest start from the latest start. Never add them. Float is in the same unit as the times, such as days or hours.
Worked example: an activity has an earliest start of 6 days and a latest start of 10 days. Float = 10 − 6 = 4 days.
A float of 4 days means the activity can start up to 4 days late and the project still finishes on time. A float of 0 means there is no room to delay it.
